With her powerhouse voice, dazzling costumes, and infectious energy, she brought Afro-Cuban music to audiences around the world. But behind the glitter and glamour was a story of exile, reinvention, and the power of music to connect us to home— or create a new one.We follow Cruz's steps from a working-class neighborhood in Havana to the top of New York's salsa scene. Along the way, we discover the African rhythms at the heart of salsa, how a new generation of Latino musicians transformed the sound of American music, and how Celia reinvented herself into an international superstar at an age when many performers are on the B-side of their careers.This project received federal support from the Smithsonian Latino Initiative Pool, administered by the Smithsonian’s National Museum of the American Latino.Special thanks to Bobby Sanabria for being our musical guide. episodes.title: Are your body clocks off? Meet ‘circadian depression’
episodes.description: What if depression is sometimes linked to your body’s internal sense of time? That’s what researchers from the University of Sydney’s Brain and Mind Centre wanted to know. In a new study, they...
episodes.description_full:
What if depression is sometimes linked to your body’s internal sense of time? That’s what researchers from the University of Sydney’s Brain and Mind Centre wanted to know. In a new study, they surveyed patients with depression whose symptoms may reflect problems with their circadian rhythms – like their sleep schedule, how tired they feel in the morning and whether they’re a night owl. They found that about 1 in 4 qualified for what might be termed a circadian subtype of depression. And while there’s still a lot of research to be done, this could open up new pathways for mental health treatment. NPR health correspondent Will Stone walks us through the study and its implications.NOTE: an earlier version of this podcast had an audio issue at 1:20 — our apologies! if you’re not hearing Gina’s question, try redownloading the episode.

episodes.description_full:
As the incoming chairman of the Oversight Committee, Representative Robert Garcia will be leading the investigations into the Trump administration’s alleged corruption.

One challenge Democrats like Garcia will face is that there simply is so much to investigate: shady crypto schemes, ballroom donations, lucrative business deals associated with Trump family members, whatever’s been happening in Venezuela. Where do you begin? And how do you deal with an administration you know is going to fight you at every turn?

So I wanted to have Garcia on the show to talk about what — and who — he wants his committee to investigate, and how these investigations fit into the Democrats’ broader strategy as they take back control of Congress.

episodes.title: How Hard Is It to Get Off Antidepressants?
episodes.description: How hard is it to get off antidepressants? Online, patients tell stories of going through hell when they stopped taking antidepressants: dizziness, brain zaps, panic attacks, anxiety and terror. And...
episodes.description_full:
How hard is it to get off antidepressants? Online, patients tell stories of going through hell when they stopped taking antidepressants: dizziness, brain zaps, panic attacks, anxiety and terror. And Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has talked about this, saying members of his family have had a worse time getting off of SSRIs than heroin. But there’s another side to this story: Lots of doctors and psychiatrists say they've been prescribing antidepressants for years and have seen many patients come off the meds with no worries. Plus, they say they have the data on their side. To find out what the science can tell us, we’re joined by Noam Hassenfeld, host of Vox’s Unexplainable, and we hear from psychiatrist Professor Philip Mitchell, Psychopharmacologist Professor David Taylor, training psychiatrist Dr Mark Horowitz, epidemiological psychiatrist Professor Glyn Lewis, and physician Professor Katharine Wallis.

This episode does mention depression. Here are some crisis hotlines:

Australia: Lifeline 13 11 14 (Online chat available)

Canada: Call or text 988

episodes.description_full: Having just experienced humanity’s latest pandemic, you might wonder when (not if) the next one is coming. Many public health experts believe we have entered into a new age of pandemics, where globalization, land use change, and climate change will increase the risk of pathogen spillover and spread. To shed light on what the future might hold, it could help to turn to the past, to the world’s first pandemic. In Pox Romana: The Plague that Shook the Roman World, Dr. Colin Elliott, Professor of History at Indiana University, presents a scoping and captivating account of the mysterious pandemic that helped to topple the Roman Empire. Using a diversity of evidence, ranging from historical accounts to archaeological remains, climatological research to economic reports, Dr. Elliott paints a richly detailed portrait of an empire on the brink of collapse and exposes the vulnerabilities allowing this pandemic to inflict the extensive damage it did. We remember how the world responded to Covid; how did ancient Romans react to the devastation of this disease? Tune in to find out. episodes.description_full: Tian Yang, CIO and manager of the VPX fund at Variant Perception, recently published a report called The Sovereign Impossible Trinity that is especially salient right now. Yang's thesis is that the US-China rivalry is exposing three main policy trade-offs: The necessity of sovereignty (which both of the great powers insist on) means that neither state can assure they can maintain the trio of guns (or the AI 'arms race'), butter (social spending), and sound money because of physical constraints, political conditions, and inflation. Given that the US-China AI arms race forms the backdrop of the upheaval at Nvidia, you can't understand Jensen Huang's resignation without considering geopolitical and global economic conditions; his leaving the chipmaker is already a world-historical story. On this episode, Yang talks to us about why Jensen might be our era's Robert Oppenheimer and what it means that the biggest powers in the world can't maintain sound monetary policy while also upholding defense and entitlements. Any effort to discourage US businesses from using Chinese open-source could be a big deal for both the AI industry and the market, where investors are still debating whether customers will ultimately be willing to pay for pricier homegrown frontier models versus cheaper alternatives. Everyone remembers last year's 'DeepSeek moment' for AI, when a Chinese company released a cheaper model that seemed nearly as good as cutting-edge US ones. He breaks down how exactly his company mixes and matches models for specific use cases, the risk of abliterated models, and the issue of data sovereignty. episodes.description_full:
Thursday, Nov. 19 will see the release of one of the biggest, most anticipated entertainment properties of the year: The video game Grand Theft Auto VI. 

The first Grand Theft Auto game was released in 1997, and immediately stoked controversy with its aggressively satirical portrait of amoral, criminal American culture. Over the past 30 years, the franchise has continued to keep a sharp satirical eye on American society, and its often unpleasant excesses. The sixth installment promises to touch on hot-button issues like the war on drugs, police violence, conspiracy theories and influencer culture. And yet, even though the game has already made one billion dollars in pre-order sales, it might be the last time we ever see one of this scale. 

In this episode of “The Sunday Daily,” Michael Barbaro talks with reporter Zachary Small, who covers video games for The Times, about Grand Theft Auto and how it became one of the biggest video game franchises of all time.
